citation: Tömmel, T. N. (2019). Love as Passion: Epistemic and Existential Aspects of Heidegger's Unknown Concept. In C. Hadjioannou (Ed.), Heidegger on Affect (Philosophers in Depth, pp. 227–244). Palgrave Macmillan. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-24639-6_10
thesis: Against the near-universal scholarly consensus that Heidegger never wrote about love, Tömmel reconstructs a rich, cross-linked concept of love from his published works, lecture courses, and especially private correspondence (with his wife Elfride, Hannah Arendt, and Elisabeth Blochmann). The chapter treats two of three possible aspects: an epistemic function, in which love (as devotion/self-abandonment, following Scheler, Augustine, and medieval mysticism) is the motivational foundation of phenomenological understanding and cognition in Heidegger's earliest writings (1912-1921), feeding into Being and Time's theory of mood as world-disclosive; and an existential function, in which love, reconstructed from the 1920s correspondence, offers an alternative, non-solipsistic path to authenticity (Eigentlichkeit) structurally parallel to being-towards-death, developed via Heidegger's engagement with Pauline messianism into a 'kairologic' concept of love as intensified, eternity-deferring temporality rather than lived duration. A third, interpersonal/social aspect of love (volo ut sis) is explicitly bracketed as outside this volume's brief. The chapter closes by arguing both aspects share one claim across all periods -- love is essentially linked to truth -- while contesting Karl Jaspers' verdict that Heidegger's philosophy was 'without love,' and closing with two reservations: Heidegger's messianic model of intimacy marginalizes the beloved, and his equation of thinking with love reads uncannily against the Black Notebooks, where his actual passion was hate. The chapter contains only one brief, negative mention of boredom and no engagement whatsoever with Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics.

sections.title: Unheaded introduction — the Black Notebooks and the justifiability of studying Heidegger; the chapter's stated aim to reconstruct his unknown concept of love

Heidegger on Love — the exclusion-consensus (Pattison) and its challengers (Derrida, Agamben); range of sources; the epistemic/existential structure; the bracketed third, interpersonal aspect (volo ut sis)

From Logic to the Logic of the Heart: Heidegger's Early Works — 1912-1921 writings; Scheler's Liebe und Erkenntnis; love/eros as motivational foundation of phenomenological understanding; transition into BT's Befindlichkeit; the SZ 139n1 footnote on Pascal/Augustine; later echoes

Love as an Alternative Path to Eigentlichkeit — the Eigentlichkeit/Mitsein tension; the 1925 wedding speech; love reconstructed from the Arendt/Blochmann letters as a second path to authenticity; the kairologic structure shared with being-towards-death; Pauline messianism; love's temporality (Augenblick vs. chronos); Scheu (shyness); passion vs. affect; rebuttal of Rentsch on positive vs. negative moods

Conclusion — love essentially linked to truth across all periods; response to Jaspers ('without love'); two closing reservations (messianic marginalization of the beloved; the uncanny love/hate equation against the Black Notebooks)
Endnotes 1-5 — cross-references to Tömmel 2013; German-original citations

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: direct but brief and negative: 'boredom and aversion' and 'being routine' named as the classical enemies of love that Heidegger's messianic/kairological concept structurally excludes

constructs.label: temporality of boredom (time-drag)
constructs.treatment: not the chapter's own claim; analogical bridge only (P/anticipatory-application) -- love's kairotic, eternity-deferring temporality functions as boredom's structural photographic negative

readings.text: Heidegger's earliest writings (1912-1921) show a shift, during the 1916 habilitation, from a fervent defense of pure logic toward phenomenology, hermeneutics, axiology, and medieval mysticism, grounding metaphysical inquiry in 'personal experience.'

The habilitation's final chapter marks the transition from logic to a Pascalian 'logic of the heart'; medieval thinking is described as 'absolute devotion' (Hingabe) and 'immersion,' graspable only through empathic understanding.

Agamben first identified Max Scheler's 1916 essay 'Liebe und Erkenntnis' as decisive for Heidegger's love-cognition link; Scheler held love the 'uniting source of consciousness' underlying cognition, perception, and willing.

1919-1920 lecture notes name love the 'motivational foundation' (Motivgrund) of phenomenological understanding, necessarily given in its 'enactmental sense' (Vollzugssinn); 'in love there is understanding.'

Heidegger criticizes Plato for treating eros as mere motivator rather than philosophy's essence; the true philosophical attitude is self-releasement into life's originality (Ursprünglichkeit), later termed Gelassenheit -- reached, on Tömmel's argument, already in 1916.
This early epistemic theory of love is the prologue to BT's theory of moods as world-disclosive: Dasein's openness is constituted by Befindlichkeit, such that there is no 'pure beholding.'

BT itself names love directly in footnote 139n1, quoting Pascal and Augustine on entering truth only through charity/loving before knowing -- linking love and truth within the published work, not only private writing.

The love-truth conviction persists into later work: 'What Is Called Thinking?' plays Vermoegen/moegen to argue thinking requires liking (loving) one's object, Being; elsewhere thinking and loving are identified outright.

Eigentlichkeit's pairing with existential isolation (reached via withdrawal from others) creates an apparent conflict with Mitsein, leading some (Großmann) to doubt whether Heidegger's 'methodological solipsism' allows authentic sociality at all.

Tömmel argues this doubt is unjustified, citing Heidegger's 1925 wedding speech for his brother: true love grows from inner truthfulness toward oneself, which then makes truthfulness toward the other possible -- consistent with BT's sequence (self first, then others anew).

Analysis of the private correspondence (chiefly Arendt 1925, Blochmann 1918-19) reveals an alternative path to authenticity alongside BT's self-centered route: the encounter with the beloved as itself a source of true selfhood.

Central interpretive claim: being-in-love and being-towards-death share the same 'kairologic structure,' developed by Heidegger through his 1919 engagement with Pauline messianism and transferred to his own philosophy.

Love's beginning is a 'true break-out' transforming existence for good, decades before Ereignis becomes central; this 'moment of vision' (Augenblick) breaks the linearity of time, paralleling Tillich's contemporaneous kairos as 'irruption of eternity into time.'

Love functions as principium individuationis like anxiety/death in BT: unlike every other undertaking, which has conventions and aids, love alone forces one into one's innermost existence -- but here individuation occurs through relation to another Dasein, not withdrawal from all others.

The Nietzsche lectures distinguish 'passion' (Leidenschaft, rooted in pathos/paschein -- to suffer, endure, be determined by) from 'affect' (Affekt, which causes loss of self); a genuine passion like love is the break-out of something already nurtured within, so receptivity does not undermine authenticity.

Love reconciles with BT's account of Dasein as burdened: love is a 'sweet burden' the lover cannot divest herself of; relating to what she is not, she comes to herself for the first time -- intensification, not annihilation, of identity.

Love's temporality is repetition (via awaiting and 'holding-out'/Durchhalten) of the founding moment of vision, not lived duration together; unlike BT's authentic having-been (repetition, SZ 385), love's repetition occurs entirely within Dasein's immanence, not as shared temporal life.

This temporal structure is messianic: the lover's condition mirrors the believer awaiting Christ's return; the 'returning unification' does not lie in future chronological time but beyond time, in eternity.

Presence-in-absence is achieved through 'shyness' (Scheu): a reserved, patient remembrance that keeps the beloved near precisely by keeping them distant; true unification heightens rather than dissolves this shyness.

Tömmel rebuts Rentsch's claim that 'positive' moods (joy, love) cannot disclose finitude as well as 'negative' ones; her analysis shows Heidegger's love is a radical loneliness, producing the same individuating effect as anxiety.

What unifies the epistemic and existential aspects across all periods is one claim: love is essentially linked to truth -- to cognition/understanding early on, to Eigentlichkeit in the 1920s, to the relation to Being later.

Against Jaspers' verdict that Heidegger's philosophy was 'without love,' Tömmel judges this philologically wrong: the sources show a highly sophisticated concept of love, on which Heidegger even identifies philosophy with love.

Two closing reservations: modeling intimacy on Pauline messianism sacralizes and marginalizes the beloved (evidence of Heidegger's inattention to interaction/community); and the thinking-is-love equation reads uncannily against the Black Notebooks, where his actual passion was hate.

letting-be; the condition of thinking Heidegger derives (per Tömmel, already in 1916) from the true philosophical/erotic attitude of self-releasement
originality/primordiality; what philosophy releases itself into, as opposed to life's mere surface
state-of-mind/attunement; BT's existential structure of world-disclosure via mood, into which the early love-epistemology feeds
authenticity/being-oneself; Heidegger's Marburg-period achievement, here shown to have an alternative, love-based route alongside anxiety/death

the moment of vision; an exceptional, rupturing temporal event that breaks with chronological linearity -- love's temporal form, on Tömmel's reading, and structurally parallel to authentic being-towards-death
being-able-to-await; the repetitious making-present, in love, of the beloved's return, sustaining the kairotic moment within everyday life
shyness/awe; the attitude toward the beloved that preserves nearness precisely by preserving distance

passion (rooted in pathos/paschein -- suffering, enduring, being determined by) vs. affect (joy, wrath -- causing loss of self); Heidegger's Nietzsche-lecture distinction used to show receptivity does not undermine authenticity

interlocutors.name: Martin Heidegger
interlocutors.role: primary corpus under analysis: early Freiburg lecture courses, Being and Time, Nietzsche lectures, 'Letter on Humanism,' 'What Is Called Thinking?', and extensive private correspondence with Elfride, Arendt, and Blochmann

interlocutors.name: Max Scheler
interlocutors.role: author of 'Liebe und Erkenntnis' (1916), identified by Agamben as decisive influence on Heidegger's love-cognition link; source of the 'love as uniting source of consciousness' formula

interlocutors.name: Giorgio Agamben
interlocutors.role: one of two prior challengers to the 'Heidegger never wrote on love' consensus; first identified the Scheler influence ('The Passion of Facticity,' 2008)

interlocutors.name: Jacques Derrida
interlocutors.role: the other prior challenger to the exclusion-consensus (Of Spirit, 1989)

interlocutors.name: George Pattison
interlocutors.role: source of the 'systematically excluded' claim that frames the chapter's motivating consensus, which Tömmel sets out to overturn

interlocutors.name: Hannah Arendt
interlocutors.role: primary correspondent/beloved (letters 1925-1975) whose exchanges with Heidegger are the chief evidential basis for the existential/kairological reconstruction; also later critic, noting Heidegger made 'desertedness productive'

interlocutors.name: Elisabeth Blochmann
interlocutors.role: second key correspondent (1918-1969), whose 1919 letter on the 'grace-character of life' supplies the account of preparing for and integrating kairotic moments into ongoing life

interlocutors.name: Andreas Großmann
interlocutors.role: raises the doubt that Heidegger's 'methodological solipsism' precludes authentic sociality, which Tömmel argues against via the 1925 wedding speech

interlocutors.name: Paul Tillich
interlocutors.role: contemporaneous theorist of kairos as 'irruption of eternity into time,' cited as parallel to Heidegger's account of love's temporal rupture

interlocutors.name: Thomas Rentsch
interlocutors.role: claims 'positive' moods (joy, love) cannot disclose finitude as well as 'negative' ones; explicitly rebutted by Tömmel's analysis of love as radical loneliness

interlocutors.name: Karl Jaspers
interlocutors.role: close friend of Heidegger who judged his philosophy 'without love'; Tömmel argues this is philologically incorrect

interlocutors.name: Michael Schmidt
interlocutors.role: cited for the phrase 'socio-ontological deficits' of Heidegger's analysis of Dasein, which the chapter's existential-aspect reconstruction aims to partially redress

interlocutors.name: Peter Trawny
interlocutors.role: author of the Black Notebooks scholarship (Jewish World Conspiracy) that frames the chapter's opening justification for continuing to study Heidegger

interlocutors.name: Günter Figal
interlocutors.role: cited for Eigentlichkeit as Heidegger's best-known Marburg-period achievement

interlocutors.name: Valeria Piazza
interlocutors.role: cited alongside Tömmel's own 2013 monograph for texts indicating Heidegger identified philosophy with love

tensions.label: Did Heidegger ever write about love?
tensions.poles: the 'systematically excluded' consensus (Pattison 2006) vs. Tömmel's (and Derrida's, Agamben's) counter-reading that love is cross-linked throughout the corpus and the leitmotiv of the private correspondence

tensions.label: Does BT's methodological solipsism preclude authentic sociality?
tensions.poles: Großmann's doubt that withdrawal-based authenticity leaves no room for genuine being-with vs. Tömmel's answer (via the 1925 wedding speech and the letters) that an alternative, love-based path to authenticity exists alongside BT's self-centered one

tensions.label: Anxiety/death vs. love as principium individuationis
tensions.poles: BT's official position that only anxiety and being-towards-death individuate Dasein vs. the 'alternative path' Tömmel reconstructs from the letters, in which love performs the identical individuating function through relation to another Dasein rather than withdrawal

tensions.label: Do 'positive' moods disclose finitude as well as 'negative' ones?
tensions.poles: Rentsch's claim that positive moods (joy, love) are structurally weaker disclosers of finitude than negative ones (anxiety, boredom) vs. Tömmel's rebuttal that Heidegger's love is in fact a radical loneliness with the same individuating force as anxiety

tensions.label: Does recovering Heidegger's concept of love make his thought or persona more 'amiable'?
tensions.poles: the possibility that a rich concept of love might soften Heidegger's post-Black-Notebooks image vs. Tömmel's own answer -- no, because the messianic model marginalizes the other and the thinking-is-love equation is uncanny set against his demonstrated hate
